summary: All 48 R1 findings checked. 39 confirmed, 9 corrected, none wrong or unreachable. Perseus (Smyth) returned a 403 cookie wall, so Smyth §§1154/1156/1168, 2346d and 3028 were checked in the archive.org scan of the same 1920 edition (agreekgrammarfo02smytgoog). Jan, Musici scriptores Graeci, was checked in the archive.org OCR, with page images n301, n358 and n365 viewed. Hiller's Theon was checked in the OCR and the page image of p. 70 (n91). Plutarch was read on Perseids CTS (Bernardakis). LSJ, DGE, Bailly and Pape came from the Logeion API, Jannaris from the archive.org OCR, Thayer from bibliaparalela, and the witness lines from the evidence files. Corrections: (1) Nicomachus Ench. 11 is Jan p. 257.7-10 and Meibom p. 21, not 22. (2) In Bacchius (Jan p. 293), Jan's note says the note names survive only in M and he doubts they are ancient; it does not say "one branch". (3) Place 05: μόνως follows μέση; it does not stand between παρυπάτη μέσων and μέση, and Xylander's asterisk is before μέση. (4) Bailly μόνως cites only Xenophon, so it supports a classical word, not a later one. (5) Plutarch, An. procr. 1021e, uses the 16:17:18 split to argue that neither part is a semitone; this tells against the "how" of place 06 index 5. (6) Plutarch, Is. 42: the text Bernardakis prints is «διαιρεῖ τὸν ἐπόγδοον λόγον εἰς ἄνισα διαστήματα τεμνόμενος»; «κατὰ τὸν» is the reading of W in his apparatus. (7) The ξκ compounds are each single attestations, in astrological, tactical, astronomical, metrical and scholiastic texts; "widespread … mathematical" overstates them. Not verifiable under the rules (no searching on the text's own witnesses): the dates of H (AD 1040), the 1532 princeps and Bas. 1556. The transcriptions themselves match the evidence files.

Perseus returned 403, so I used the 1920 edition on archive.org (same numbering). §1154 defines the attributive position, §1156 says that words preceded by the article have attributive position, and §1168 gives the predicate position. None of them treats an anarthrous noun and participle, so the claim that they are neutral holds.

LSJ I.3: «value at a certain price, ὁπόσης ἂν τιμῆς ἀξιώσῃ τὸ πωλούμενον Pl. Lg. 917d». This is the genitive of price, a related but separate sense, so it is a parallel and not proof.

Checked in the archive.org scan because Perseus returned 403. Smyth: «In prose hyperbaton is less common than in poetry, but even in prose it is frequent», and the displacement usually gives prominence to the first word. The example D. 18.158 is given.

H 64v.11, Par. 21r.19 and V 76r.11 have εἰ γὰρ; Bas. 24.23 has εἰ δὲ μὴ. The dates 1532 and 1556 are not in the evidence file and could not be checked.

§2346d: «εἰ δὲ μή (but if not …) otherwise. In alternatives.» N.1: «εἰ δὲ μή often occurs even where the preceding clause is negative and we expect εἰ δέ». The remark about compositors is labelled correctly as the researcher's inference.

Bas. 26.1 «εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡ μονάς»; P fr. 1, Vinc. 338.4 «Εἰ γὰρ καὶ τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς»; εἰ δέ for alternatives at Bas. 31.21-22, 32.9 and 32.15.

checks.correction: μόνως does not stand between παρυπάτη μέσων and μέση. It follows μέση («παρυπάτη μέσων, * μέση μόνως, παράμεσος»), and Xylander's asterisk is printed before μέση. The text says «διὰ τούτων ἀπαρτίζεται τὸ ἐν πεντεκαιδεκαχόρδῳ ἑκκαιδεκάχορδον»; it does not say simply that the list makes up the πεντεκαιδεκάχορδον. The 1:8 = 8:15 statement is at Bas. 25.14-17.

checks.correction: The 'how' misrepresents Plutarch. He doubles 9:8 to 18:16 and takes 17 between them only to show that the epogdoon is divided unequally, and he concludes «οὐδέτερον ἄρα γίγνεται … τῶν τμημάτων ἡμιτόνιον». He attests the arithmetic 16:17:18 division, but denies that 17:16 is a semitone. He is therefore no witness for an established doctrine of 8½:8 as the semitone.

checks.correction: Each form is a single attestation. They come from astrological (Ps.-Ptol.), tactical (Ael.), astronomical (Plu. Fac.), scholiastic (Sch. Ar.) and metrical (Heph.) texts, and none is a mathematical treatise. They show that the ξκ spelling is attested in late technical Greek; 'widespread … including mathematical' overstates this.
